claim: Development and homeostasis of multicellular organisms is largely controlled by complex cell-cell signaling networks that rely on specific binding of secreted ligands to cell surface receptors.
source: Development and homeostasis of multicellular organisms is largely controlled by complex cell-cell signaling networks that rely on specific binding of secreted ligands to cell surface receptors.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about cell-cell signaling in multicellular organisms.

claim: The Wnt signaling network involves multiple ligands and receptors to elicit specific cellular responses.
source: The Wnt signaling network, as an example, involves multiple ligands and receptors to elicit specific cellular responses.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about the Wnt signaling network.

claim: The method presented delivers precise equilibrium dissociation coefficients of interactions in the Wnt signaling pathway.
source: Here, we present a robust approach based on fluorescence correlation spectroscopy with ultra-high speed axial line scanning, yielding precise equilibrium dissociation coefficients of interactions in the Wnt signaling pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript showing KD measurements.

claim: Using CRISPR/Cas9 editing to endogenously tag receptors with fluorescent proteins, the method delivers precise results even with low, near-native amounts of receptors.
source: Using CRISPR/Cas9 editing to endogenously tag receptors with fluorescent proteins, we demonstrate that the method delivers precise results even with low, near-native amounts of receptors.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing KD measurements on CRISPR/Cas9 edited cells with low receptor densities.

claim: Wnt signaling is an ancient and evolutionarily conserved, complex network that controls a variety of physiological processes essential for embryonic development and tissue homeostasis.
source: Among these, Wnt signaling is an ancient and evolutionarily conserved, complex network that controls a variety of physiological processes essential for embryonic development and tissue homeostasis (Clevers and Nusse, 2012; Niehrs, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: There are 10 different Frizzled G-protein-coupled receptors binding 19 different Wnt glycolipoprotein ligands in humans.
source: There are 10 different Frizzled G-protein-coupled receptors binding 19 different Wnt glycolipoprotein ligands (in humans), and additional co-receptors and effector proteins are also crucially involved in the modulation of signal transduction (Niehrs, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The equilibrium dissociation coefficient, KD, determines the fraction of ligand-bound receptors at a particular ligand concentration.
source: Accordingly, the equilibrium dissociation coefficient, KD, which determines the fraction of ligand-bound receptors at a particular ligand concentration, should be measured for all relevant interactions in the network.
evidence: This is a statement of established biophysical knowledge.

claim: In vitro assays may not completely emulate the complex environment of living cells and tissues.
source: Those assays, however, may not completely emulate the complex environment of living cells and tissues; consequently, researchers are striving to measure biomolecular interactions as closely as possible to the real-life situation (Ries et al., 2009b; Ng et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature discussing the limitations of in vitro assays.

claim: Fluorescence correlation spectroscopy (FCS) is a powerful method for measuring ligand-receptor interactions within the plasma membrane of live cells.
source: Fluorescence correlation spectroscopy (FCS) is a powerful method for measuring ligand-receptor interactions within the plasma membrane of live cells (Bacia et al., 2006; Ries et al., 2009b; Dörlich et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on FCS applications.

claim: Line-scanning FCS (lsFCS) solves the problem of cell membrane movement by quickly scanning the observation volume perpendicularly through the membrane.
source: Line-scanning FCS (lsFCS) solves this problem by quickly scanning the observation volume perpendicularly through the membrane (Ries et al., 2009a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature on lsFCS.

claim: The poor photostability of GFP-like proteins poses a challenge because the focused laser spot causes local photobleaching.
source: The poor photostability of GFP-like proteins poses yet another challenge because the focused laser spot causes local photobleaching.
evidence: This is a statement of known properties of GFP-like proteins.

claim: Axial line scanning with a TAG lens allows sweeping the observation volume through the membrane within a few microseconds, more than two orders of magnitude faster than with lateral line scanning by galvanometric scanners.
source: In contrast to earlier approaches (Ries et al., 2009a; Ries et al., 2009b; Dörlich et al., 2015), we employ axial (i.e. along the optical axis) line scanning at ultra-high speed by using a tunable acoustic gradient index of refraction (TAG) lens (Duocastella et al., 2014). This device allows us to sweep the observation volume through the membrane within a few microseconds and thus more than two orders of magnitude faster than with lateral line scanning by means of galvanometric scanners.
evidence: This is supported by the technical description of the TAG lens and comparison to lateral scanning.

claim: With axial lsFCS, the correlation decay is significantly faster than with lateral lsFCS, resulting in shorter overall measurement times to reach comparable precision.
source: With axial lsFCS, the correlation decay is significantly faster than with lateral lsFCS, resulting in shorter overall measurement times to reach comparable precision.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing axial and lateral lsFCS shown in Figure 2.

claim: The much higher scanning frequency of TAG lens-based axial lsFCS results in an enhanced time resolution of the correlation functions.
source: Moreover, the much higher scanning frequency of TAG lens-based axial lsFCS results in an enhanced time resolution of the correlation functions.
evidence: This is inferred from the technical properties of the TAG lens and the resulting correlation functions.

claim: In dual-color cross-correlation experiments, optimal overlap of the observation volumes is much easier to achieve with axial lsFCS.
source: In dual-color cross-correlation experiments, optimal overlap of the observation volumes is much easier to achieve with axial lsFCS.
evidence: This is inferred from the technical properties of axial scanning compared to lateral scanning.

claim: In vitro studies determined KD values in the range of 0.3–0.5 nM (without error analysis) for DKK1 and DKK2 binding to LRP6.
source: For these interactions, KD values in the range of 0.3–0.5 nM (without error analysis) were determined by in vitro studies (Bafico et al., 2001; Mao et al., 2001; Semënov et al., 2001); a more recent paper reported 3 ± 1 nM (Bourhis et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature reporting these KD values.

claim: A more recent paper reported a KD of 3 ± 1 nM for DKK1/DKK2 binding to LRP6.
source: For these interactions, KD values in the range of 0.3–0.5 nM (without error analysis) were determined by in vitro studies (Bafico et al., 2001; Mao et al., 2001; Semënov et al., 2001); a more recent paper reported 3 ± 1 nM (Bourhis et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The receptor density in the plasma membrane was varied in the range 20–1000 µm–2 by using three different ways to express LRP6 receptors fused to fluorescent proteins.
source: To explore this issue, we varied the receptor density in the plasma membrane in the range 20–1000 µm–2 by using three different ways to express LRP6 receptors fused to fluorescent proteins in the cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing receptor densities measured by axial lsFCS.

claim: There is impressive consistency in the KD determinations using LRP6 fused to mCherry and tdTomato markers, which differ considerably in size, brightness and emission spectrum.
source: We have observed an impressive consistency in the KD determinations using LRP6 fused to mCherry and tdTomato markers, which differ considerably in size, brightness and emission spectrum (Shaner et al., 2005), attesting to the accuracy of the results.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing KD values obtained with different fluorescent markers.

claim: The home-built microscope uses three available lasers (blue (470 nm), green (561 nm) and red (640 nm)), pulsing every 25 ns with a mutual delay of 12.5 ns.
source: For dual-color excitation, we select two out of three available lasers (blue (470 nm), green (561 nm) and red (640 nm)), pulsing every 25 ns with a mutual delay of 12.5 ns.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental setup.

claim: The pulsed interleaved excitation scheme yields two time-separated intervals of 12.5 ns during which photons are collected in two color channels, strongly reducing channel crosstalk.
source: This pulsed interleaved excitation scheme (Müller et al., 2005) yields two time-separated intervals of 12.5 ns during which photons are collected in two color channels; channel crosstalk is thus strongly reduced.
evidence: This is supported by the technical description of the excitation scheme and a citation to prior literature.

claim: A TAG lens driven in resonance (147 kHz) moves the observation volume up and down along the optical axis by several micrometer in an oscillatory manner with a period of ~6.8 µs.
source: In addition, we use a TAG lens driven in resonance (147 kHz) to move the observation volume up and down along the optical axis by several micrometer in an oscillatory manner with a period of ~6.8 µs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the technical description and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Axial lsFCS data can be visualized as kymographs, displaying the intensity during the axial sweeps along the x-axis and multiple sweeps in succession along the y-axis.
source: These data can be visualized as kymographs, displaying the intensity during the axial sweeps along the x-axis and multiple sweeps in succession along the y-axis (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by the description and Figure 2c showing a kymograph.

claim: The autocorrelation function from axial lsFCS can be fitted very well with a model function based on a circular observation area in the x-y plane and 2D diffusion within the membrane.
source: From the intensity time trace, we calculate an autocorrelation function, which can be fitted very well with a model function based on a circular observation area in the x-y plane and 2D diffusion within the membrane (Figure 2d)
evidence: This is supported by the fit shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Axial lsFCS has several advantages over lateral scanning, resulting in a markedly reduced data acquisition time for comparable data quality.
source: To conclude, axial lsFCS has several advantages over lateral scanning, resulting in a markedly reduced data acquisition time for comparable data quality (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is supported by the comparison shown in Figure 2e.

claim: An overall shorter measurement is less likely to be spoiled by sample movement, which is unavoidable in experiments on live specimens.
source: Notably, an overall shorter measurement is less likely to be spoiled by sample movement, which is unavoidable in experiments on live specimens.
evidence: This is inferred from the properties of live cell imaging.

claim: The unavoidable intrinsic background fluorescence of live samples and photobleaching of the markers during the experiment can severely compromise the analysis of FCS data.
source: Notably, the unavoidable intrinsic background fluorescence of live samples and photobleaching of the markers during the experiment can severely compromise the analysis of FCS data.
evidence: This is a statement of known challenges in live cell FCS experiments.

claim: There is only a small and insignificant change of the resulting KD parameter from 0.08 ± 0.01 nM to 0.10 ± 0.02 nM, with and without background correction, respectively.
source: Indeed, there is only a small and insignificant change of the resulting KD parameter from 0.08 ± 0.01 nM to 0.10 ± 0.02 nM, with and without background correction, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The different types of gene insertion yield widely different LRP6-mCherry receptor densities at the cell membrane, ranging from 18 µm–2 for the CRISPR/Cas9 edited cells to ~1000 µm–2 for strongly overexpressing HEK293T cells.
source: In any case, it is evident that the different types of gene insertion yield widely different LRP6-mCherry receptor densities at the cell membrane, ranging from 18 µm–2 for the CRISPR/Cas9 edited cells to ~1000 µm–2 for strongly overexpressing HEK293T cells.
evidence: This is supported by the receptor density data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: KD values of 0.08 ± 0.01 and 0.09 ± 0.01 nM were found for cell lines harboring stably integrated LRP6-mCherry and CRISPR/Cas9 edited cells.
source: We find KD values of 0.08 ± 0.01 and 0.09 ± 0.01 nM for cell lines harboring stably integrated LRP6-mCherry and CRISPR/Cas9 edited cells, whereas three- to fourfold lower affinities are observed for transiently transfected cells.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 6 and Table 1.

claim: Three- to fourfold lower affinities are observed for transiently transfected cells compared to stably integrated and CRISPR/Cas9 edited cells.
source: We find KD values of 0.08 ± 0.01 and 0.09 ± 0.01 nM for cell lines harboring stably integrated LRP6-mCherry and CRISPR/Cas9 edited cells, whereas three- to fourfold lower affinities are observed for transiently transfected cells.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 6 and Table 1.

claim: Binding of DKK1-eGFP and DKK1-eGFP-SNAP to the receptors yielded essentially identical results, with KD = 0.49 ± 0.09 and 0.46 ± 0.09 nM, respectively.
source: Axial lsFCS experiments were carried out using HEK293T cells transiently overexpressing LRP6-mCherry. Binding of DKK1-eGFP and DKK1-eGFP-SNAP to the receptors yielded essentially identical results (Figure 6 and Table 1), with KD = 0.49 ± 0.09 and 0.46 ± 0.09 nM, respectively, suggesting that the fusion tag perturbs the interaction only in a very minor way.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 6 and Table 1.

claim: The fusion tag perturbs the DKK1-LRP6 interaction only in a very minor way.
source: Binding of DKK1-eGFP and DKK1-eGFP-SNAP to the receptors yielded essentially identical results (Figure 6 and Table 1), with KD = 0.49 ± 0.09 and 0.46 ± 0.09 nM, respectively, suggesting that the fusion tag perturbs the interaction only in a very minor way.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar KD values obtained with different fusion constructs.

claim: DKK2 has been reported to have a lower affinity toward LRP6 than DKK1.
source: DKK2 has been reported to have a lower affinity toward LRP6 than DKK1 (Mao et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The KD for DKK2 binding to LRP6 is 0.26 ± 0.04 nM, indicating a significantly reduced affinity with respect to DKK1 binding (KD = 0.08 ± 0.01 nM).
source: Indeed, our result, KD = 0.26 ± 0.04 nM, for DKK2 indicates a significantly reduced affinity with respect to DKK1 binding to stably transfected NCI-H1703 cells (KD = 0.08 ± 0.01 nM, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2 and Table 2.

claim: For LRP6-tdTomato fusion constructs, KD values of 0.10 ± 0.02 and 0.22 ± 0.03 nM were obtained for DKK1 binding to CRISPR/Cas9 gene edited and transiently transfected cells, respectively.
source: For LRP6-tdTomato fusion constructs, we obtained KD values of 0.10 ± 0.02 and 0.22 ± 0.03 nM for DKK1 binding to CRISPR/Cas9 gene edited and transiently transfected cells, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3 and Table 2.

claim: The KD values obtained for LRP6-tdTomato are identical within the error to those obtained for LRP6-mCherry.
source: These values are identical within the error to those obtained for LRP6-mCherry.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of the data in Tables 1 and 2.

claim: The larger size of the tdTomato label does not adversely affect DKK1 binding.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that (i) the larger size of the tdTomato label does not adversely affect DKK1 binding and (ii) we can reliably measure affinities in the subnanomolar range in live cells even with less bright fluorescent protein tags such as mCherry.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar KD values obtained with mCherry and tdTomato labels.

claim: Affinities in the subnanomolar range can be reliably measured in live cells even with less bright fluorescent protein tags such as mCherry.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that (i) the larger size of the tdTomato label does not adversely affect DKK1 binding and (ii) we can reliably measure affinities in the subnanomolar range in live cells even with less bright fluorescent protein tags such as mCherry.
evidence: This is supported by the successful KD measurements using mCherry-tagged receptors.

claim: Kremen proteins were originally identified as negative regulators of Wnt signaling.
source: They were originally identified as negative regulators of Wnt signaling (Mao et al., 2002; Ellwanger et al., 2008), amplifying DKK-mediated inhibition of Wnt signaling.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Formation of a ternary complex of DKK, LRP6 and Kremen was proposed, which is rapidly endocytosed and thereby depletes the Wnt co-receptor LRP6 from the plasma membrane.
source: Formation of a ternary complex of DKK, LRP6 and Kremen was proposed, which is rapidly endocytosed and thereby depletes the Wnt co-receptor LRP6 from the plasma membrane (Mao et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: In the absence of DKK, Kremen proteins have been reported to enhance Wnt signaling by stabilizing the LRP6 receptor at the plasma membrane via Kremen-LRP6 heterodimer formation.
source: In the absence of DKK, however, Kremen proteins have also been reported to enhance Wnt signaling by stabilizing the LRP6 receptor at the plasma membrane via Kremen-LRP6 heterodimer formation (Hassler et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Axial lsFCS yielded a KD value of 10.3 ± 2.1 nM for DKK1 binding to xKremen2-mCherry.
source: Consistent with this observation, axial lsFCS yielded a KD value of 10.3 ± 2.1 nM (Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplement 2, Table 2), which is considerably higher than the previously reported in vitro values of <3 nM for DKK1 binding to mKremen2 (Mao et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplement 2, and Table 2.

claim: The KD of 10.3 ± 2.1 nM for DKK1 binding to xKremen2 is considerably higher than the previously reported in vitro values of <3 nM for DKK1 binding to mKremen2.
source: Consistent with this observation, axial lsFCS yielded a KD value of 10.3 ± 2.1 nM (Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplement 2, Table 2), which is considerably higher than the previously reported in vitro values of <3 nM for DKK1 binding to mKremen2 (Mao et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of the measured KD with values from prior literature.

claim: When unlabeled LRP6 was co-expressed together with xKremen2-mCherry, the apparent affinity of DKK1-eGFP toward xKremen2-mCherry increased roughly 20-fold (KD = 0.54 ± 0.06 nM).
source: However, when unlabeled LRP6 was co-expressed together with xKremen2-mCherry, there was pronounced green staining of the plasma membrane by DKK1-eGFP already at ligand concentrations below 1 nM (Figure 7—figure supplement 1b). This effect was not a result of a markedly higher xKremen2-mCherry concentration in the membrane because axial lsFCS revealed an xKremen2-mCherry density of 68 ± 10 µm–2 with and 79 ± 11 µm–2 without LRP6 co-expression, respectively (Figure 7a). Instead, the apparent affinity of DKK1-eGFP toward xKremen2-mCherry was found to increase roughly 20-fold (KD = 0.54 ± 0.06 nM) in the presence of co-expressed, unlabeled LRP6 (Figure 7b).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 7 and Table 2.

claim: LRP6, xKremen2 and DKK1 engage in a ternary complex, with DKK1 binding mediated mainly by the receptor with higher affinity, that is LRP6.
source: This finding suggests that LRP6, xKremen2 and DKK1 indeed engage in a ternary complex, with DKK1 binding mediated mainly by the receptor with higher affinity, that is LRP6.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased affinity observed upon LRP6 co-expression.

claim: DKK1 binding within the LRP6-DKK1-xKremen2 complex is not as strong as to LRP6 alone (KD = 0.22 ± 0.02 nM), presumably because the presence of Kremen interferes with the optimal formation of DKK1-LRP6 binding interfaces.
source: DKK1 binding within the LRP6-DKK1-xKremen2 complex is not as strong as to LRP6 alone (KD = 0.22 ± 0.02 nM, see Table 1), presumably because the presence of Kremen interferes with the optimal formation of DKK1-LRP6 binding interfaces.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of KD values with and without Kremen co-expression.

claim: 25 ± 14% of LRP6 receptors co-diffused with the more abundant xKremen2 receptor, that is they were part of a dual-labeled receptor heterodimer.
source: We found that 25 ± 14% of LRP6 receptors co-diffused with the more abundant xKremen2 receptor, that is they were part of a dual-labeled receptor heterodimer; 15 ± 6% of the xKremen2 receptors co-diffused with LRP6 (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: 15 ± 6% of the xKremen2 receptors co-diffused with LRP6.
source: We found that 25 ± 14% of LRP6 receptors co-diffused with the more abundant xKremen2 receptor, that is they were part of a dual-labeled receptor heterodimer; 15 ± 6% of the xKremen2 receptors co-diffused with LRP6 (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: KD values between 0.08 and 10 nM have been measured, and it is estimated that it will be possible to extend this range by about one more order of magnitude.
source: In the investigations presented here, we have measured KD values between 0.08 and 10 nM and we estimate that it will be possible to extend this range by about one more order of magnitude, making the method broadly applicable to a wide range of ligand-receptor interactions.
evidence: This is based on the experimental data and speculation about future capabilities.

claim: The method is not limited to cultured cells but can also study tissue samples or model organisms.
source: Notably, we are not limited to cultured cells but can also study tissue samples or model organisms.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential applicability of the method.

claim: Axial scanning offers clear advantages over lateral scanning; most importantly, it features a smaller observation area of circular shape on the plasma membrane of cells.
source: Axial scanning offers clear advantages over lateral scanning; most importantly, it features a smaller observation area of circular shape on the plasma membrane of cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the technical properties of axial scanning.

claim: The overall data acquisition time can be reduced by about five-fold with respect to lateral scanning for comparable data precision.
source: As a consequence, the overall data acquisition time can be reduced by about five-fold with respect to lateral scanning for comparable data precision, and the unavoidable changes in cell position and morphology are less likely to compromise the measurements.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Data could be collected at receptor densities as low as ca. 20 µm‒2, using CRISPR/Cas9-edited NCI-H1703 cells expressing endogenously tagged receptors.
source: Data could be collected at receptor densities as low as ca. 20 µm‒2, using, CRISPR/Cas9-edited NCI-H1703 cells expressing endogenously tagged receptors.
evidence: This is supported by the receptor density data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Wild-type (wt) cells appear to express even lower levels of LRP6 than the endogenously tagged CRISPR/Cas9 edited cells, as judged from comparative western blot analysis.
source: Wild-type (wt) cells appear to express even lower levels of LRP6 than the endogenously tagged CRISPR/Cas9 edited cells, as judged from comparative western blot analysis.
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The CRISPR/Cas9 edited cells express the single (heterozygous) targeted allele of LRP6 at higher levels than both LRP6 alleles in wt cells.
source: The CRISPR/Cas9 edited cells express the single (heterozygous) targeted allele of LRP6 at higher levels than both LRP6 alleles in wt cells.
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The endogenously tagged allele of CRISPR/Cas9 edited cells is also expressed at higher levels than the corresponding untagged allele.
source: The endogenously tagged allele of CRISPR/Cas9 edited cells is also expressed at higher levels than the corresponding untagged allele.
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The increased expression of endogenously tagged LRP6 may result from removal and/or displacement of micro-RNA binding sites present in the 3' untranslated region, which function as negative regulatory elements for LRP6 expression.
source: Possibly, the increased expression of endogenously tagged LRP6 may result from removal and/or displacement of micro-RNA binding sites present in the 3' untranslated region, which function as negative regulatory elements for LRP6 expression (Zhang et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to prior literature on miRNA regulation of LRP6.

claim: Subnanomolar equilibrium binding coefficients of eGFP labeled DKK1 and DKK2 ligands binding to LRP6 receptors tagged with mCherry and tdTomato at the C-terminus were determined, in agreement with earlier in-vitro studies.
source: In agreement with earlier in-vitro studies (Bafico et al., 2001; Mao et al., 2001; Semënov et al., 2001; Bourhis et al., 2010), we determined subnanomolar equilibrium binding coefficients of eGFP labeled DKK1 and DKK2 ligands binding to LRP6 receptors tagged with mCherry and tdTomato at the C-terminus.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data and citations to prior literature.

claim: The KD values of DKK1-LRP6 binding were found to increase noticeably with increasing apparent receptor density, from 0.08 nM at 20–50 µm‒2 to 0.5 nM at ~1000 µm‒2.
source: The KD values of DKK1-LRP6 binding were found to increase noticeably with increasing apparent receptor density, from 0.08 nM at 20–50 µm‒2 to 0.5 nM at ~1000 µm‒2.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 6 and Tables 1 and 2.

claim: Such an affinity modulation could result from receptor-receptor interactions, which become more prevalent at higher density.
source: Such an affinity modulation could result from receptor-receptor interactions, which become more prevalent at higher density.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed density-dependent affinity changes.

claim: Local LRP6 densities can be much higher if the receptors segregate into nanodomains embedded within the observation area of 0.2 µm2.
source: However, local LRP6 densities can be much higher if the receptors segregate into nanodomains embedded within our observation area of 0.2 µm2.
evidence: This is speculation about possible receptor clustering.

claim: There is ample evidence for LRP6 clustering from a range of studies.
source: Unfortunately, direct visualization of LRP6 clustering is precluded by the diffraction-limited resolution of our confocal microscope, but there is ample evidence for such clustering from a range of studies.
evidence: This is supported by inference from prior literature on LRP6 clustering.

claim: A LRP6 variant lacking the entire ectodomain is constitutively active in the absence of Wnt ligands.
source: Interestingly, a LRP6 variant lacking the entire ectodomain composed of four 300-residue long, concatenated modules (PE1–4), each containing a YWTD β-propeller and an epidermal growth factor (EGF)-like domain, followed by three LDLR type A modules (LA1–3) of 40 residues each, is constitutively active in the absence of Wnt ligands (Mao et al., 2001; Liu et al., 2003; Brennan et al., 2004; Chen et al., 2014; Ren et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: For a variety of engineered ectodomain variants, the level of signaling activity was found to scale inversely with the size of the ectodomain.
source: Moreover, for a variety of engineered ectodomain variants, the level of signaling activity was found to scale inversely with the size of the ectodomain (Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: There is an intrinsic tendency of the LRP6 transmembrane (TM) domain to oligomerize, leading to spontaneous signaling upon LRP6 overexpression.
source: Matoba et al., 2017 argued that there is an intrinsic tendency of the LRP6 transmembrane (TM) domain to oligomerize, leading to spontaneous signaling upon LRP6 overexpression.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The curved shape of the bulky ectodomain on the cell surface keeps the TM domains apart and thus counteracts oligomerization and spontaneous signaling.
source: The curved shape of the bulky ectodomain on the cell surface, which they visualized by negative stain electron microscopy, presumably keeps the TM domains apart and thus counteracts oligomerization and spontaneous signaling.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: This repulsive effect may be relieved by conformational rearrangements straightening the ectodomain upon formation of LRP6-Wnt-Frizzled complexes.
source: This repulsive effect may be relieved by conformational rearrangements straightening the ectodomain upon formation of LRP6-Wnt-Frizzled complexes (Matoba et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: DKK binding would stabilize the bent form of the ectodomain.
source: By contrast, DKK binding would stabilize the bent form of the ectodomain.
evidence: This is inferred from the discussion of LRP6 ectodomain conformations.

claim: A higher LRP6 expression level could presumably lead to denser packing of the bulky LRP6 ectodomain, giving it less freedom to adopt the curved shape favorable for DKK binding, which then may cause the reduced affinity toward DKK antagonists at higher LRP6 expression levels.
source: Thus, in our experiments, a higher LRP6 expression level could presumably lead to denser packing of the bulky LRP6 ectodomain, giving it less freedom to adopt the curved shape favorable for DKK binding, which then may causes the reduced affinity toward DKK antagonists at higher LRP6 expression levels.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed density-dependent affinity changes and prior knowledge of LRP6 structure.

claim: The DKK1-LRP6-xKremen complex appears to be mainly stabilized by interactions between DKK1-LRP6 and Kremen-LRP6, but not significantly by the weaker DKK1-xKremen2 interaction (KD = 10.3 ± 2.1 nM).
source: Thus, the DKK1-LRP6-xKremen complex appears to be mainly stabilized by interactions between DKK1-LRP6 and Kremen-LRP6, but not significantly by the weaker DKK1-xKremen2 interaction (KD = 10.3 ± 2.1 nM).
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of KD values for different interactions.

claim: This scenario implies a mutual interaction between the two receptors, which was confirmed by axial lsFCS experiments on cells expressing both receptors labeled in different colors, showing a high degree of heterodimer formation.
source: This scenario implies a mutual interaction between the two receptors, which was confirmed by axial lsFCS experiments on cells expressing both receptors labeled in different colors, showing a high degree of heterodimer formation.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: Even small changes in KD values can be measured, attesting to the robustness and reliability of the method.
source: Our investigations show that even small changes in KD values can be measured, attesting to the robustness and reliability of the method.
evidence: This is supported by the consistency of KD measurements across different experimental conditions.

claim: Incomplete fluorophore maturation in the fluorescent protein tag is a source of systematic error.
source: Two sources of such errors, namely (1) incomplete fluorophore maturation in the fluorescent protein tag, and (2) lack of binding competence of a fraction of ligands or receptors, and their effects on the data have been discussed in the Materials and methods section.
evidence: This is discussed in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Lack of binding competence of a fraction of ligands or receptors is a source of systematic error.
source: Two sources of such errors, namely (1) incomplete fluorophore maturation in the fluorescent protein tag, and (2) lack of binding competence of a fraction of ligands or receptors, and their effects on the data have been discussed in the Materials and methods section.
evidence: This is discussed in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The accuracy hinges on the precise knowledge of the ligand concentration in the CM.
source: Finally, we note that the accuracy hinges on the precise knowledge of the ligand concentration in the CM.

claim: The TAG lens is driven in resonance at 147 kHz.
